Stacked on #174 (`audit/lang-c-data-members`), not on `main`. #174 rewrites exactly the code this touches and explicitly defers this half — its `fieldDeclNames` comment reads *"A plain function declarator names nothing here: `int Add(int);` in a class body is a method declaration, not data, and is left to the entity walk."* This is the entity walk.

## The defect

A C++ header exists to hold declarations. The class body declares constructors, a destructor, and const / static / noexcept / override members; the definitions live in the `.cpp` as `Type::method`. **None of those declarations were extracted.**

A nine-member class produced one method symbol:

```
class:Ledger  method:Ledger.Inline  field:Ledger.total_  field:Ledger.handler_
```

`Ledger()`, `~Ledger()`, `Add`, `Version`, `Reset`, `Over` — all absent. Only the one member with an inline body survived. So a class written the way C++ is normally written contributed no method symbols at all: nothing to search for, no `CONTAINS` edge, and nothing for a typed receiver to resolve a call to.

## Why it was invisible

tree-sitter-cpp gives an in-class method declaration no node type of its own:

| source | node type |
|---|---|
| `int Add(int) const;` | `field_declaration` — the same node as `int total_;` |
| `Ledger();` / `~Ledger();` | `declaration` — the same node as a local variable |
| `int Inline(int x) { … }` | `function_definition` — the only one already handled |

Neither `field_declaration` nor `declaration` reached any case in `entityFromNode`.

## The fix

Two conditions separate a member declaration from everything sharing those node types:

1. It sits directly in a `field_declaration_list` — the class body. That excludes locals, namespace-scope prototypes, and the `declaration` nested inside a `friend_declaration`, none of which are members.
2. Its declarator resolves to a `function_declarator` whose own declarator is a **name**. A function-pointer data member (`int (*handler_)(int);`) reaches a `parenthesized_declarator` instead and stays the field #174 classifies it as.

Members are marked `bodyless` in the field's existing sense: the declaration is real — it is where the parameter types are written — but the out-of-line definition is the definition, so `bodylessOverloadImplementation` still resolves an overload set to the implementation.

## Operator overloads are deliberately excluded

`maskCPlusPlusOperatorCall` rewrites `operator=(` into a same-length `op(` before tree-sitter sees the file, while entity text is read back from the **unmasked** source. The parsed name is therefore a prefix of the written one, and every masked operator collapses onto the same stand-in — `operator=` and `operator==` on one class would both be extracted as `Ledger.op`, two members under one name.

The guard is general rather than special-cased: `cFamilyNameEndsAtTokenBoundary` rejects any name whose node range does not end at a token boundary in the entity source, so any mask that shortens an identifier is caught, not just this construct. Recovering real operator names belongs with the mask.

## Verification

Three tests, three mutations, each killed by a different one:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| hook disabled in `entityFromNode` | `TestCPlusPlusInClassMethodDeclarationsAreExtracted` — 7 missing symbols |
| `field_declaration_list` parent guard dropped | `…StaysInClassBodies` — extracts `method:Ledger.Peek` from a `friend` declaration |
| token-boundary guard dropped | `…OperatorDeclarationsStayUnextracted` — extracts `method:Ledger.op` |

`go test ./...`, `go vet ./...` and `gofmt -s -l` are clean, and no golden fixture moved.

Two trail findings on trail 135.

01M19RTCCCM7 -- methodsByContainer is keyed by NAME, so C++ overloads collide
in it, and last-write-wins made the winner depend on source order. With
`void f(int) { ... }` followed by `void f(double);`, the bodyless declaration
replaced the inline definition, every `obj.f(...)` resolved to the
declaration, and the real implementation was left with no callers -- impact
on working code reported nothing. A bodyless entry no longer displaces one
that has a body; the reverse still applies, which is what lets an
out-of-line definition replace a declaration indexed before it.

01M19E7J6FXK -- cPlusPlusOutOfLineDefinition matched `Container::Name` with
strings.Contains, which is wrong in both directions. It matched too much
(`BA::foo` contains `A::foo`, so an unrelated class's definition was accepted
as the body and emitted a CALLS edge to the wrong function) and too little (a
template definition is spelled `A<T>::foo` and never contains the bare text,
so those calls stayed pointed at the declaration). Both are the same mistake:
treating a qualified name as text rather than as tokens. The match now
requires token boundaries on both ends and qualifies through a template
argument list.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): keep a body in the method index, and match qualified names …","oid":"0b5413056dba6abdf428204f926255bb027bae67"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-03T01:25:27Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-03T01:25:27Z","messageBody":"maskCPlusPlusOperatorCall replaced the operator token with a fixed `op`
stand-in that preserved the width of the whole MATCH but not of the
operator's own NAME: `operator=` (9 chars) became `op` (2). Symbol names
are sliced from the unmasked source at the parsed node's byte range, so
the slice read the wrong bytes back, and every masked operator collapsed
onto the same `op`. Bodyless operator overloads were therefore dropped
entirely rather than risk two symbols sharing one name.

Pad the stand-in with '_' to the width of the operator name, so it stays
a single identifier token and the byte range slices back the real
spelling. `Ledger& operator=(const Ledger&);` now yields
`Ledger.operator=`, and `=`/`==`/`!=` on one class stay distinct.

An in-class allocation or deallocation member — `void* operator new(size_t)`,

word, so maskCPlusPlusOperatorCall (which requires punctuation between

those members produced no symbol at all: nothing to search for, no
CONTAINS edge, no call target. Read the name back off the node's own
range, which for an unrewritten operator still holds the real spelling,
and refuse anything that no longer reads as an operator name rather than
emitting a stand-in.

Stacked on #174 (`audit/lang-c-data-members`), not on `main`. #174 rewrites exactly the code this touches and explicitly defers this half — its `fieldDeclNames` comment reads *"A plain function declarator names nothing here: `int Add(int);` in a class body is a method declaration, not data, and is left to the entity walk."* This is the entity walk.

## The defect

A C++ header exists to hold declarations. The class body declares constructors, a destructor, and const / static / noexcept / override members; the definitions live in the `.cpp` as `Type::method`. **None of those declarations were extracted.**

A nine-member class produced one method symbol:

```
class:Ledger  method:Ledger.Inline  field:Ledger.total_  field:Ledger.handler_
```

`Ledger()`, `~Ledger()`, `Add`, `Version`, `Reset`, `Over` — all absent. Only the one member with an inline body survived. So a class written the way C++ is normally written contributed no method symbols at all: nothing to search for, no `CONTAINS` edge, and nothing for a typed receiver to resolve a call to.

## Why it was invisible

tree-sitter-cpp gives an in-class method declaration no node type of its own:

| source | node type |
|---|---|
| `int Add(int) const;` | `field_declaration` — the same node as `int total_;` |
| `Ledger();` / `~Ledger();` | `declaration` — the same node as a local variable |
| `int Inline(int x) { … }` | `function_definition` — the only one already handled |

Neither `field_declaration` nor `declaration` reached any case in `entityFromNode`.

## The fix

Two conditions separate a member declaration from everything sharing those node types:

1. It sits directly in a `field_declaration_list` — the class body. That excludes locals, namespace-scope prototypes, and the `declaration` nested inside a `friend_declaration`, none of which are members.
2. Its declarator resolves to a `function_declarator` whose own declarator is a **name**. A function-pointer data member (`int (*handler_)(int);`) reaches a `parenthesized_declarator` instead and stays the field #174 classifies it as.

Members are marked `bodyless` in the field's existing sense: the declaration is real — it is where the parameter types are written — but the out-of-line definition is the definition, so `bodylessOverloadImplementation` still resolves an overload set to the implementation.

## Operator overloads are deliberately excluded

`maskCPlusPlusOperatorCall` rewrites `operator=(` into a same-length `op(` before tree-sitter sees the file, while entity text is read back from the **unmasked** source. The parsed name is therefore a prefix of the written one, and every masked operator collapses onto the same stand-in — `operator=` and `operator==` on one class would both be extracted as `Ledger.op`, two members under one name.

The guard is general rather than special-cased: `cFamilyNameEndsAtTokenBoundary` rejects any name whose node range does not end at a token boundary in the entity source, so any mask that shortens an identifier is caught, not just this construct. Recovering real operator names belongs with the mask.

## Verification

Three tests, three mutations, each killed by a different one:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| hook disabled in `entityFromNode` | `TestCPlusPlusInClassMethodDeclarationsAreExtracted` — 7 missing symbols |
| `field_declaration_list` parent guard dropped | `…StaysInClassBodies` — extracts `method:Ledger.Peek` from a `friend` declaration |
| token-boundary guard dropped | `…OperatorDeclarationsStayUnextracted` — extracts `method:Ledger.op` |

`go test ./...`, `go vet ./...` and `gofmt -s -l` are clean, and no golden fixture moved.

## Language matrix (#171)

This is the last of the three changes that close the C++ `CALLS` gap #171 audits. Verified on a scratch merge of #171 + #174 + #176 + this branch, the matrix fixture goes from

```
relations [DEFINES CONTAINS USES_TYPE]
```

to

```
symbols   [class:Ledger field:total_ function:Add function:LedgerDouble method:Add]
relations [CALLS CONTAINS DEFINES IMPORTS USES_TYPE]
```

so the `cpp` entry in `languageMatrix` retires to:

```go
{dir: "cpp", symbols: []string{"class:Ledger", "method:Add", "field:total_", "function:LedgerDouble"}, relations: []string{"DEFINES", "CONTAINS", "CALLS", "USES_TYPE"}},
```

The matrix file lives on #171's branch, not this one, so the edit is not in this diff. It does not need chasing: `TestLanguageMatrixCallsGapsAreExactlyAsAudited` fails on a stale entry by design — *"a fix landed without the audited gap list being retired with it"* — so whichever of these merges last will surface it.

## Known residue

An out-of-line definition `int Ledger::Add(...)` is still emitted as a top-level `function:Add` rather than as `method:Ledger.Add`, so the fixture now carries both. The `CALLS` edge lands on the declaration, which is correct but less precise than landing on the definition. Two trail findings on trail 135.

01M19RTCCCM7 -- methodsByContainer is keyed by NAME, so C++ overloads collide
in it, and last-write-wins made the winner depend on source order. With
`void f(int) { ... }` followed by `void f(double);`, the bodyless declaration
replaced the inline definition, every `obj.f(...)` resolved to the
declaration, and the real implementation was left with no callers -- impact
on working code reported nothing. A bodyless entry no longer displaces one
that has a body; the reverse still applies, which is what lets an
out-of-line definition replace a declaration indexed before it.

01M19E7J6FXK -- cPlusPlusOutOfLineDefinition matched `Container::Name` with
strings.Contains, which is wrong in both directions. It matched too much
(`BA::foo` contains `A::foo`, so an unrelated class's definition was accepted
as the body and emitted a CALLS edge to the wrong function) and too little (a
template definition is spelled `A<T>::foo` and never contains the bare text,
so those calls stayed pointed at the declaration). Both are the same mistake:
treating a qualified name as text rather than as tokens. The match now
requires token boundaries on both ends and qualifies through a template
argument list.","messageHeadline":"fix(sem): keep a body in the method index, and match qualified names …","oid":"0b5413056dba6abdf428204f926255bb027bae67"},{"authoredDate":"2026-09-03T01:25:27Z","authors":[{"email":"257360244+suhaanthayyil@users.noreply.github.com","id":"U_kgDOD1cBdA","login":"suhaanthayyil","name":"Suhaan Thayyil"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-03T01:25:27Z","messageBody":"maskCPlusPlusOperatorCall replaced the operator token with a fixed `op`

operator's own NAME: `operator=` (9 chars) became `op` (2). Symbol names
are sliced from the unmasked source at the parsed node's byte range, so
the slice read the wrong bytes back, and every masked operator collapsed
onto the same `op`. Bodyless operator overloads were therefore dropped
entirely rather than risk two symbols sharing one name.

Pad the stand-in with '_' to the width of the operator name, so it stays
a single identifier token and the byte range slices back the real
spelling. `Ledger& operator=(const Ledger&);` now yields
`Ledger.operator=`, and `=`/`==`/`!=` on one class stay distinct.

Two gaps in the in-class C++ declaration work.

An in-class allocation or deallocation member — `void* operator new(size_t)`,
`void operator delete(void*)` and their array forms — is spelled with a
word, so maskCPlusPlusOperatorCall (which requires punctuation between
`operator` and the `(`) never rewrites it and the parser reports a real
`operator_name` node. That case discarded the declarator outright, so
those members produced no symbol at all: nothing to search for, no
CONTAINS edge, no call target. Read the name back off the node's own
range, which for an unrewritten operator still holds the real spelling,
and refuse anything that no longer reads as an operator name rather than
emitting a stand-in.

signatureNamesQualifiedMethod skipped a template argument list at the
first `>`. Angle brackets nest, so `A<std::vector<T>>::foo` and
`A<std::vector<T> >::foo` close the outer list at the SECOND one; cutting

      "textSnapshot": "Problem: C++ headers declare their interfaces (methods, constructors, destructors) in the class body but define those members out of line in .cpp files. Because only the out-of-line definition was extracted as a symbol, classes using header-only declarations contributed no method symbols to the graph \u2014 no way to search for method names, no CONTAINS edges from class to method, and no typed-receiver resolution for method calls.\nSolution: Extract C++ in-class method declarations as bodyless method entities. These capture the interface signature and parameter types from the header, marked with bodyless: true to indicate the definition lives elsewhere. The extractor distinguishes method declarations from similarly-shaped non-members by requiring they sit directly in a field_declaration_list (the class body), and by checking that the declarator chain resolves to a function_declarator. Operator overloads are deliberately skipped because the C++ parser masks operator= and similar constructs into a uniform op stand-in, collapsing distinct operators onto one name. Function-pointer data members are correctly left as fields, not methods, by detecting parenthesized_declarator in the chain. Four test cases verify scope boundaries (in-class only, not locals or namespace-scope prototypes), constructor/destructor/override/const extraction, and C struct members staying unaffected.",

Function-pointer data members are correctly left as fields, not methods, by detecting parenthesized_declarator in the chain. {"body":"`compound-v1` IDs cannot be stable under *both* signature edits and overload insertion/reorder. Today's C++ member-declaration scheme picks one; a review finding on #177 asks for the other. Neither is free, so this needs a decision rather than another flip.

## The contract

- `docs/semantic-provider-requirements.md:614` — "Stable `compound-v1` symbol IDs for ordinary body/signature edits."
- `AGENTS.md:224` — "`compound-v1` symbol IDs must stay stable across ordinary edits."

Both an `int` -> `long` parameter edit and adding an overload are ordinary edits.

## The two schemes, both measured on #177

**A. `#sig:<hash(signature)>` — current HEAD** (`internal/sem/provider.go:1853`, commit `2c2c9066`).
Every bodyless C++ member declaration is forced onto the collision path (`colliding = true`), so even a lone declaration carries a signature hash.

Fails a signature edit:

```
class Ledger { public: int Add(int); };    -> ...:method:Ledger.Add#sig:694fcbed86ad5d9c
class Ledger { public: int Add(long); };   -> ...:method:Ledger.Add#sig:eb1333e68d9ed488
```

Survives insertion and reorder.

**B. `#decl:<source-order ordinal>`** — commit `10146975`, reverted by `2c2c9066`; this is what the review finding asks for ("lone declarations need a signature-independent stable ID").
Survives signature edits, and fails insertion *and* reorder. Restoring `10146975`'s `provider.go` makes `TestCPlusPlusDeclarationOverloadIDsSurviveSiblingEdits` fail at `parser_cpp_member_declaration_test.go:622`:

```
insertion/reorder changed IDs:
  lone      = [<ID>]                          <- lone declaration gets the BARE id
  before    = [<ID>#decl:1 <ID>#decl:2]       <- adding an overload retires that bare id
  inserted  = [<ID>#decl:1 <ID>#decl:2 <ID>#decl:3]
  reordered = [<ID>#decl:1 <ID>#decl:2]       <- swapping two declarations swaps their ids
```

So B breaks on two edit classes where A breaks on one. B is not a strict improvement.

## Why there is no third option at this level

Overloads differ from one another in exactly two observable ways: their signature and their position. A signature-derived key dies on a signature edit; a position-derived key dies on insertion or reorder. Any purely syntactic disambiguator is one or the other, so the contract as currently written is unsatisfiable for C++ overload sets.

## The decision needed

1. Which edit class must a C++ overload-set ID survive — signature edits (B) or insertion/reorder (A)? and
2. Does the requirements wording need narrowing to say so, since it currently promises both?

An escape from the trade-off would need identity anchored outside the declaration text — e.g. a per-file identity map carried across snapshots, resolved by the existing move/rename reconciliation, rather than a syntactic suffix. That is a larger change than a finding round should make.

Until this is settled, #177 keeps scheme A and the finding is dismissed with a pointer here.

Refs: #177, `internal/sem/provider.go:1846-1866`, `internal/sem/parser_cpp_member_declaration_test.go:592-624`.

  "title": "fix(sem): extract C++ in-class method declarations",
  "body": "Problem: C++ headers declare their interfaces (methods, constructors, destructors) in the class body but define those members out of line in .cpp files. Because only the out-of-line definition was extracted as a symbol, classes using header-only declarations contributed no method symbols to the graph — no way to search for method names, no CONTAINS edges from class to method, and no typed-receiver resolution for method calls.\nSolution: Extract C++ in-class method declarations as bodyless method entities. These capture the interface signature and parameter types from the header, marked with bodyless: true to indicate the definition lives elsewhere. The extractor distinguishes method declarations from similarly-shaped non-members by requiring they sit directly in a field_declaration_list (the class body), and by checking that the declarator chain resolves to a function_declarator. Operator overloads are deliberately skipped because the C++ parser masks operator= and similar constructs into a uniform op stand-in, collapsing distinct operators onto one name. Function-pointer data members are correctly left as fields, not methods, by detecting parenthesized_declarator in the chain. Four test cases verify scope boundaries (in-class only, not locals or namespace-scope prototypes), constructor/destructor/override/const extraction, and C struct members staying unaffected.",

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-graph/trails/135

C++ classes that declare methods in headers previously contributed no method symbols for those declarations. This extracts bodyless in-class methods, constructors, destructors, templates, operator overloads, and comma-separated declarations while keeping function-pointer data members classified as fields.

Calls through declarations now redirect to a unique out-of-line definition using AST names and lexical owners, including nested classes and inline namespaces. Ambiguous overloads remain conservative, and inherited calls retain their confidence and resolution metadata. Declaration signatures and type metadata preserve template constraints and shared specifiers.

Targets main directly. The former parent, PR #174 / trail 133 (C and C++ data members), has merged. Current main is integrated without conflicts while preserving the branch's existing commits and checkpoints.

Known limitation: C++ declaration IDs use signature hashes to survive overload insertion and reordering; signature edits change those IDs. This tradeoff is tracked in #214, and its associated trail finding was explicitly dismissed pending that design decision.

Validation of the integrated branch is in progress: full Go race suite, vet, build, formatting, and status-line tests. Hosted CI and fresh trail review will be checked before merge.
EOF
